title: Two lending markets: local lender or foreign lender
summary: A loan from a lender in another country, at a lower headline rate, is not automatically cheaper for a project abroad. Where the collateral sits, which law governs it and what currency the income is in usually decide the real cost and the real risk.
body:
When a project is in one country and cheaper money is available in another, the headline rate is the least reliable guide to which is better. Mr Shabazz, the lender will lend against collateral it can register and enforce in its own system, and that decides whose assets are really at risk.

In plain English

Suppose you live in one country, call it the home country, and are building in another, the project country. A bank at home may offer a lower interest rate than any bank in the project country. It is tempting to borrow at home and spend the money abroad. But the home bank has a problem: it cannot easily take and sell a building in a foreign country under foreign law. So it will usually want security it can reach at home, such as your house or other property there, and your personal guarantee. The project's risk then sits on your home balance sheet.

The professional framing: the factors to compare

  • Who lends. Local commercial banks know the project market, its courts and its land registry. Foreign banks know you and your home assets.
  • Collateral they can take. Security over land is registered in the place the land sits, under that place's law. A foreign lender usually cannot take an effective mortgage over the project without local counsel and local registration, and may not want to.
  • Rate environment. Base rates and average lending rates differ between countries. Average figures published by central banks or data services describe the market, not what your project will be offered [unverified — confirm current rates independently].
  • Currency. A local bank may lend in the local currency or in US dollars; a foreign bank lends in its own currency or US dollars. The project's income currency may match neither. Lesson 23 covers this.
  • Tax on interest. Interest paid to a resident local bank usually carries no withholding tax; interest paid to a non-resident lender often does. Lesson 22 covers this.
  • Typical structure. Locally, a construction-to-term facility against the project. From abroad, often a loan against your home assets, re-lent or invested into the project.
  • Co-lending. In some markets, local banks lend alongside development-finance institutions on larger projects. For a single small asset this is uncommon [unverified — market-specific].

The professional framing: banks that span both markets

Some international banks operate in the project country through a local branch or subsidiary. A branch is part of the foreign parent; a subsidiary is a separate locally licensed company. Either may be a possible bridge between a relationship at home and a facility abroad, but whether it would lend on a particular project, or link the two relationships, can only be learned by asking [unverified — ask informally once your package is ready].

A worked example

Compare two hypothetical offers for a US$650,000 loan on a building abroad. All figures are illustrative.

  1. Local bank. 8.5 percent, secured on the project building, with a completion guarantee that burns off at completion. Your home assets are not pledged.
  2. Home bank. 7.0 percent, secured on your home property worth US$900,000, with a full personal guarantee. The project building is not pledged to it.
  3. On interest alone, the home bank saves 1.5 percent a year on US$650,000, about US$9,750 a year.
  4. Now ask what you are buying with that saving. If the project fails, the local bank's recovery comes from the building and is limited by the burn-off guarantee. The home bank's recovery comes from your home. You have exchanged US$9,750 a year for putting your house behind a foreign building.
  5. Before even reaching tax and currency, which the next two lessons add, the cheaper loan carries a much larger personal risk.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is silently moving the project's risk onto family assets. A home-country loan secured on a home or other property means a failure abroad is paid for at home, possibly by people who did not sign up for the project. That is a wealth-strategy and family decision as much as a financing one, and should be made deliberately, with independent advice, rather than as a side effect of chasing a lower rate.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares headline rates. "Seven percent at home beats eight and a half abroad." Compare all-in cost instead: the rate, plus any withholding-tax gross-up, plus fees, plus the cost of hedging or carrying currency risk, plus a realistic value on the personal exposure you take on. Lessons 22 and 23 show how the first two of those can close most of the gap.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, build a side-by-side table with one column per lender and rows for rate, security taken, guarantees, currency of loan, currency of income, tax on interest, fees and governing law. Fill in every row before discussing rate. Then ask the home-country lender directly what security it would take, and the local lender what it would credit as equity. Treat the answers as data about where your risk will sit. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer in each country on security and enforcement, and a tax adviser in each country on interest withholding and any treaty.

There is a timing point as well. A local lender's process may be slower and its document list longer, and a home-country lender who already knows you may move faster. Speed has value during a tight construction window, so record it in the comparison too, but do not let it decide the question of where your risk sits.

A neutral framing helps in conversations with family too. The question is not "which bank is cheaper" but "which assets are we prepared to stand behind this building, and at what price". Put that way, the choice usually becomes clear quickly.
checklist: Security over land is registered and enforced where the land sits.
A home-country lender usually lends against home-country assets and your guarantee.
Published average rates describe a market, not your offer.
Check loan currency against income currency.
Interest paid to a non-resident lender may carry withholding tax.
Compare all-in cost and where the risk sits, not headline rate.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A home-country bank offers 6.5 percent secured on your house; a project-country bank offers 8.0 percent secured on the building. What questions must you answer before choosing?
selftest.a: What security each takes and what that means if the project fails (house versus building); what guarantees each requires and whether they burn off; whether interest to the home bank is subject to withholding tax with a gross-up; whether the loan currency matches the income currency and what hedging would cost; and the fees and governing law. Only then compare all-in cost, and decide deliberately whether to put home assets behind the project.

apply: Draw a two-column comparison table for a hypothetical home lender and project-country lender with rows for rate, security, guarantees, currency, tax on interest, fees and governing law.
sources: Source: the parent handbook, Banking and Project Finance, Parts 8 and 9. Withholding tax, tax treaties, enforcement of foreign judgments and registration of security are matters of law and tax that change and differ by country; every rate or rule mentioned is [unverified — confirm independently] with a tax adviser and lawyer in each country involved. Term-sheet terms are commercial practice and negotiable.

title: Withholding tax and the gross-up: the hidden cost of foreign debt
summary: Many countries tax interest paid to a lender outside the country by withholding part of each payment. Lenders usually require a gross-up clause, so the borrower pays the tax on top and the real cost of the loan rises.
body:
When interest is paid to a lender in another country, the project country may require part of it to be withheld as tax, and a lender with a gross-up clause makes you pay that tax on top. Mr Shabazz, a gross-up turns a cheap foreign rate into an expensive one, and it is a single line in the loan agreement.

In plain English

Many countries tax income that leaves the country. When a local borrower pays interest to a foreign lender, the law may require the borrower to keep back a percentage of each payment and send it to the tax authority. This is withholding tax. The foreign lender then receives less than its agreed interest. Lenders protect themselves with a gross-up clause: the borrower must increase the payment so that, after the tax is withheld, the lender still receives the full amount. The borrower pays the tax.

The professional framing: treaties and statutory rates

Two layers of rule usually apply. The project country's own law sets a statutory withholding rate on interest paid to non-residents. A double-tax treaty between the two countries may cap that rate. Where a treaty cap is higher than the statutory rate, the lower statutory rate generally applies, because a treaty limits tax rather than creating it. As an illustration of how this is read, one published summary reports that the Canada and Guyana treaty allows Guyana to tax interest paid to a Canadian lender at up to 25 percent, and that Guyana's lower statutory rate of 20 percent therefore applies [unverified — confirm independently against the treaty text and current law with a tax adviser in both countries]. Treaties also have conditions, such as the lender being the beneficial owner of the interest, and exemptions sometimes exist for certain lenders. None of this should be relied on without advice.

The professional framing: the arithmetic

With a full gross-up, the effective rate you pay equals the agreed rate divided by one minus the withholding rate. The lender receives its agreed rate; you pay the larger figure. The lender may be able to claim a credit for the withheld tax in its own country, but that benefits the lender, not you, unless the agreement shares the credit, which is rare and worth asking about.

A worked example

Use a hypothetical 20 percent withholding rate and a full gross-up. All figures are illustrative.

  1. A foreign lender quotes 7.0 percent. Effective cost: 7.0 divided by 0.80, which is 8.75 percent. On a US$650,000 loan, interest-only for simplicity, that is about US$56,875 a year instead of US$45,500, an extra US$11,375.
  2. A foreign lender quotes 6.0 percent. Effective cost: 6.0 divided by 0.80, which is 7.5 percent.
  3. A local lender quotes 8.5 percent with no withholding, because it is resident. Effective cost: 8.5 percent.
  4. Now add the other costs of the 7.0 percent foreign loan. Arrangement fees of 1.5 percent spread over a five-year term add about 0.3 percent a year. Hedging the currency mismatch might cost around 1.0 percent a year [illustrative only — hedging costs vary widely]. All-in: about 8.75 plus 0.3 plus 1.0, roughly 10.05 percent.
  5. The local loan, with 1.0 percent of fees over five years, is about 8.7 percent all-in.

The loan quoted 1.5 points cheaper is about 1.35 points more expensive once withholding, fees and hedging are counted, and it still carries the collateral and guarantee issues of the previous lesson.

The professional framing: coverage effects

The gross-up is part of debt service. A lender sizing the loan, and you testing coverage, must include the grossed-up payments. A project that covers debt service 1.30 times at the quoted rate could fall to roughly 1.10 times or lower once a 20 percent gross-up is added, depending on how much of each payment is interest rather than principal, enough to fail a covenant that looked comfortable.

The professional framing: structures that change the answer

Because the tax follows the lender's residence and the form of the payment, structure can change it. A loan from a lender resident in the project country carries no withholding. A loan routed through an entity in a third country, or a home-country loan to you personally that you then invest as equity rather than lend onward, may be taxed differently, and may raise other issues, including anti-avoidance rules that look through artificial arrangements. These choices are squarely for tax advisers in each country, and every one of them interacts with how the bank counts equity, which Week 4 covered. The point for you is to ask the question before the structure is fixed, not after the first interest payment is due.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a change in tax law or treaty status after you sign. Gross-up clauses usually put the risk of a future increase in withholding on the borrower. If the rate rises, your cost rises with it, and there is no cap unless you negotiate one or a right to prepay without penalty if a gross-up is triggered.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the interest rate and skips the tax clause. Every cross-border loan agreement has a section on taxes and increased costs; read it first, not last, and model it in the coverage test.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, for any lender outside the project country, ask three questions in writing before negotiating rate: is interest subject to withholding, is there a gross-up, and can the lender claim relief that it would share? Then compute the effective rate as the quoted rate divided by one minus the withholding rate, add fees and hedging, and compare all-in. Ask for a prepayment right without penalty if a gross-up is triggered or increased. Professional sign-off required: tax advisers in both countries; lawyer on the tax and increased-costs clauses.
checklist: Withholding tax is deducted from interest paid to a non-resident lender.
A treaty may cap the rate; a lower statutory rate generally applies where it is lower.
A gross-up makes the borrower pay the tax on top.
Effective rate equals quoted rate divided by one minus the withholding rate.
Include gross-up in debt service when testing coverage.
Negotiate a penalty-free prepayment right if a gross-up is triggered.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A foreign lender quotes 6.0 percent with a full gross-up, and interest is subject to a 20 percent withholding. A local lender quotes 7.2 percent with no withholding. Which is cheaper on interest alone?
selftest.a: The foreign loan's effective rate is 6.0 divided by 0.80, which is 7.5 percent, more than the local 7.2 percent. The local loan is cheaper on interest before even counting fees, hedging, and the collateral and guarantee differences. The withholding rate itself must be confirmed with tax advisers.

apply: Compute the effective rate of a hypothetical foreign loan at three quoted rates under a 15 and a 20 percent withholding, with full gross-up.

title: Currency mismatch: when the debt and the rent speak different languages
summary: If a loan is in one currency and the building's income is in another, an exchange-rate move can break the coverage ratio without the building performing any worse. Lenders stress this, and so should you.
body:
Borrowing in one currency against income in another adds a risk that has nothing to do with the building: the exchange rate. Mr Shabazz, a 10 percent currency move can do to your coverage ratio what a 10 percent rent cut would, and it can happen in weeks.

In plain English

Your tenants pay rent in one currency. Your loan payments are due in another. Each month you convert rent into the loan currency. If the rent currency weakens against the loan currency, the same rent buys less of the loan currency, and your payments become harder to meet. Nothing changed in the building. The tenants paid in full. The coverage ratio still fell.

The professional framing: types of mismatch

  • Income in a local currency, debt in a foreign one. The classic danger: if the local currency weakens, debt service grows in local terms.
  • Income in US dollars, debt in a third currency. Even where rents are in US dollars, a loan in, say, Canadian dollars still carries the US dollar to Canadian dollar rate.
  • Costs in one currency, income in another. Construction costs paid in imported materials and foreign-currency contracts can rise while local rents stay flat.
  • Pegs and managed rates. Some currencies are held close to a fixed rate by a central bank. A peg reduces day-to-day movement but can be adjusted, sometimes sharply. Always use the current official published rate in a model rather than an old fixed figure carried from an earlier document, and record the date of the rate used.

The professional framing: managing it

  1. Match the currencies. Borrow in the currency the building earns. This is the cleanest answer and the one lenders prefer.
  2. Write leases in the loan currency, where local law and the market allow.
  3. Hedge. Forward contracts or currency swaps fix the exchange rate for a period, at a cost, and may not be available for long periods or small amounts in thinner currencies.
  4. Hold a reserve in the loan currency large enough to absorb a defined move.
  5. Size the loan to a stressed rate, so coverage holds after a defined adverse move.

A worked example

Hypothetical figures only. A loan in Canadian dollars requires annual debt service of C$85,000. The building's NOI is US$80,000 a year. The exchange rate at signing is US$1 to C$1.35.

  1. NOI in loan currency: US$80,000 times 1.35 is C$108,000. DSCR: C$108,000 divided by C$85,000 is about 1.27 times. It clears 1.20 times.
  2. The US dollar weakens 11 percent, to US$1 to C$1.20. NOI in loan currency: US$80,000 times 1.20 is C$96,000.
  3. DSCR: C$96,000 divided by C$85,000 is about 1.13 times. The covenant is breached. The building collected every dollar of rent.
  4. Combine it with a 10 percent fall in NOI, to US$72,000: C$86,400 against C$85,000, about 1.02 times, barely covering payments at all.

If the loan had been in US dollars, step 2 would have changed nothing. That is the case for matching.

The professional framing: what the lender will ask

A lender facing a currency mismatch will typically ask four things. What currency are the leases written in, and can tenants legally be required to pay in another? What exchange-rate stress does the coverage survive? Is a hedge available, for how long and at what cost, and will the hedge counterparty rank with or behind the bank? And is there a reserve in the loan currency? If the borrower cannot answer, the lender will often reduce the loan to a level that survives its own stress, which may be a larger cut than the borrower would have chosen voluntarily.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is correlation. Currency weakness in a project country often arrives with a weaker local economy, which also lowers rents and occupancy. The two stresses tend to come together, not one at a time, so test them together, as in step 4 above.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner models one exchange rate, today's, for the whole life of the loan, sometimes an out-of-date rate copied from an old document. Model a range, use the current official rate with its date, and show coverage at the worst point of that range.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, write down three currencies for every project: the currency of costs, of income and of debt. If they are not all the same, compute coverage at today's official rate and at a rate 15 and 25 percent worse, alone and combined with a 10 percent NOI fall. If coverage fails in the combined case, either match the loan currency to income, hedge, hold a reserve or borrow less. Treat a lender's currency stress as a check on yours, not a substitute. Professional sign-off required: a treasury or foreign-exchange adviser for any hedge, and a lawyer on currency and payment clauses.

A practical point on records: whenever an exchange rate appears in a model or a memo, write the source and the date beside it. A rate without a date is a number nobody can check, and an old rate in a new document is one of the commonest errors a lender's analyst finds.

There is also a timing dimension. During construction, costs are often paid in a mix of currencies as materials are imported, while the loan is drawn in one currency, so the mismatch can bite before a single tenant moves in. Ask your cost consultant which budget lines are priced in foreign currency, and hold contingency against those lines specifically. Once the building operates, the mismatch moves from costs to income, and the reserve and stress tests above take over.
checklist: Write down the currency of costs, income and debt for every project.
A weaker income currency raises debt service in local terms without any change in the building.
Matching the loan currency to income is the cleanest answer.
Hedges fix the rate at a cost and may be unavailable for long periods or small amounts.
Use the current official rate with its date, never an old fixed figure.
Test currency and NOI stress together; they tend to arrive together.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Your loan is in euros with annual debt service of 90,000 euros. NOI is US$120,000 and today US$1 buys 0.85 euros. What is DSCR now, and after the dollar weakens to 0.75 euros?
selftest.a: Now: US$120,000 times 0.85 is 102,000 euros, so DSCR is 102,000 divided by 90,000, about 1.13 times. After the move: US$120,000 times 0.75 is 90,000 euros, DSCR exactly 1.00 times, with no cushion at all. The loan is already thin at today's rate and fails a typical covenant; matching the currency or borrowing less is indicated.

apply: For a hypothetical project, list the currency of costs, income and debt, and compute coverage at today's rate and at a rate 15 percent worse.

title: Decoding a term sheet
summary: A term sheet is the bank's offer of terms; almost every clause can be negotiated before you sign it and almost none after. Read it as a list of risks you are agreeing to carry.
body:
A term sheet lists the terms a lender is offering, and it is the last cheap moment to change them. Mr Shabazz, read each clause by asking what risk it puts on you, and push back before signing, because the loan agreement will be drafted from it.

In plain English

A term sheet is a short document, often a few pages, setting out the main terms of a proposed loan. A commitment letter is the bank's formal offer after credit approval. The loan agreement is the long legal document that follows. Each step narrows the room to negotiate. A term sheet is usually not binding, except for fees and confidentiality. A commitment letter is usually binding on the bank, subject to its conditions. Neither is the loan agreement, and neither moves money.

The professional framing: the clauses

ClausePush forRed flag
Facility amountSized to the binding test with headroomAn amount "up to" with no sizing basis
PurposeInterest reserve, soft costs and contingency includedLand or soft costs excluded without warning
Interest rateFixed or capped during constructionFloating, uncapped, on a tight coverage ratio
FeesCredited at closing; no exit fee on refinanceFees payable even if the bank later declines
Term and amortisationLonger amortisation; interest-only during buildA short balloon soon after completion
Drawdown conditionsCost-consultant certification, clear timelinesBank discretion to refuse draws
Equity requirementLand credited at appraisal; equity pro rataAll equity first, valued at cost
SecurityLimited to the project and borrowing companyCross-collateral over your other assets
GuaranteesCompletion guarantee that burns offUnlimited personal guarantee for the term
Financial covenantsTested on stabilised NOI, with cure rightsTested from day one, no cure
Conditions precedentA realistic list you can deliverItems outside your control
PrepaymentFree after a short periodHeavy penalty blocking a refinance
Material adverse changeNarrow, objective definitionBroad wording that lets the bank walk away
ExpiryEnough time to satisfy conditionsExpiry before approvals can land
Governing lawLocal law for local securityMismatch between loan law and security law

The professional framing: what usually moves, and what does not

Not every clause is equally negotiable. Pricing, fees, the equity credit for land, the guarantee structure, the prepayment terms and the expiry date are often movable, especially for a well-prepared borrower or one with competing offers. Core credit tests, such as the minimum coverage ratio and loan-to-cost limit, and core security requirements, such as a first mortgage, move far less, because they come from the bank's credit policy rather than from the relationship manager. Concentrate your counters where movement is likely, and on the clauses that carry the most risk for you, rather than spreading effort evenly across every line.

The professional framing: how to read it

Read the term sheet three times. First for money: amount, rate, fees, term, amortisation, and what each costs per year. Second for control: conditions precedent, drawdown conditions, covenants, events of default and material adverse change, which together decide when the bank can stop funding. Third for personal exposure: security, guarantees, cross-collateral and governing law. Many borrowers read only the first pass.

A worked example

A hypothetical term sheet offers US$650,000 at a floating base rate plus 3.0 percent, currently 8.0 percent in total, with a 1.0 percent arrangement fee and a 0.5 percent commitment fee both payable on signing the term sheet and non-refundable, a 24-month term with a balloon, and all equity first valued at cost.

  1. Fees. 1.5 percent of US$650,000 is US$9,750, payable now, even if the bank later declines. Push for the fees to be payable at closing or credited against closing.
  2. Floating rate. Coverage is 1.33 times at 8.0 percent. A two-point rise takes debt service on a 25-year basis to about US$70,900 and coverage to about 1.13 times. Push for a cap or a fixed rate during construction.
  3. Balloon. A 24-month term on an 18-month build leaves six months to lease up and refinance. Push for a longer term or an extension option on defined conditions.
  4. Equity at cost. Land bought for US$100,000 and appraised at US$140,000 is credited at US$100,000. Ask for appraisal credit; US$40,000 of equity is at stake.

Four lines in a short document carried US$9,750 of fee risk, a covenant breach on a two-point rate rise, a refinancing cliff and US$40,000 of equity.

Notice that none of these four items is unusual, and none is necessarily a reason to refuse the bank. Each is a negotiating point with a price. Sometimes the bank will move; sometimes it will not, and you must decide whether to accept the risk, mitigate it yourself or look elsewhere.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is the material adverse change clause and its relatives, any wording that lets the bank decline to fund at its discretion. A loan the bank can refuse to advance whenever it becomes nervous is not a commitment; it is an option held by the bank. Narrow it to objective tests.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner pays a non-refundable commitment fee before checking whether every condition precedent can actually be met. If title is unresolved or approvals are pending, the fee may be lost. Check every condition against what legally exists today before paying.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, mark up every term sheet in three colours for money, control and personal exposure, and write beside each clause the risk it puts on you and your counter. Send counters in one consolidated letter, prioritised, rather than piecemeal. Professional sign-off required: your own lawyer before signing any term sheet or commitment letter, and before paying any non-refundable fee.
checklist: A term sheet is usually non-binding except fees and confidentiality.
A commitment letter is the bank's binding offer, subject to its conditions.
Read three times: money, control, personal exposure.
Watch for floating uncapped rates, balloons, cross-collateral and broad material-adverse-change wording.
Check every condition precedent against what exists today before paying fees.
Send counters in one prioritised letter.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A term sheet requires a non-refundable 1 percent commitment fee on signing and lists as a condition precedent written planning approval, which you expect in four months, with the offer expiring in three. What do you do?
selftest.a: Do not pay yet. The expiry falls before a condition you cannot control can be met, so the fee is at risk. Ask for the expiry to be extended past the expected approval date with margin, for the fee to be payable at closing or refundable if the condition cannot be met, or for the condition to be restructured; have your lawyer review before signing.

apply: Mark up any sample term-sheet clause list in three groups (money, control, personal exposure) and write one counter-proposal for each group.

title: Week 5 review: cross-border borrowing and the term sheet
summary: Six questions on comparing lending markets, withholding tax, currency mismatch and term-sheet clauses. Work each aloud before reading the answer.
body:
This week tested the habit of looking past the headline rate: where the collateral sits, what tax and currency add, and what each term-sheet clause commits you to. Mr Shabazz, work each question aloud before reading the answer.

Question 1. Why can a 7 percent home-country loan cost more than an 8.5 percent project-country loan for a project abroad?

Answer. Because interest paid to a non-resident lender may be subject to withholding tax, which a gross-up clause makes you pay on top; because borrowing in a currency different from the building's income adds exchange-rate risk and possibly hedging cost; and because fees differ. At a hypothetical 20 percent withholding, 7 percent becomes 8.75 percent before fees and hedging. The home loan is also likely to be secured on your home assets with a full guarantee, a personal cost not shown in the rate at all.

Question 2. Where is security over land registered, and what does that mean for a foreign lender?

Answer. In the place where the land sits, under that place's law. A foreign lender cannot easily take or enforce an effective mortgage over a building abroad without local counsel and registration, so it usually lends against assets it can reach at home and your personal guarantee. The project's risk then moves onto your home balance sheet.

Question 3. Calculation. A loan is quoted at 6.0 percent, interest to the lender is subject to 20 percent withholding, and there is a full gross-up. What is the effective cost?

Answer. 6.0 divided by one minus 0.20, which is 6.0 divided by 0.80, equals 7.5 percent. The withholding rate used here is illustrative and must be confirmed with tax advisers in both countries.

Question 4. A loan's debt service is C$85,000 a year and NOI is US$80,000. At US$1 to C$1.35 coverage is about 1.27 times. What happens at US$1 to C$1.20, and what is the cleanest fix?

Answer. NOI becomes C$96,000 and coverage falls to about 1.13 times, breaching a 1.20 times covenant although every dollar of rent was collected. The cleanest fix is to borrow in the currency the building earns. Alternatives are writing leases in the loan currency, hedging at a cost, holding a reserve in the loan currency, or sizing the loan to a stressed rate.

Question 5. What is the difference between a term sheet and a commitment letter, and which clauses decide when the bank can stop funding?

Answer. A term sheet is usually non-binding except for fees and confidentiality; a commitment letter is the bank's binding offer after credit approval, subject to its conditions. Neither is the loan agreement. The clauses that decide when funding can stop are the conditions precedent, the drawdown conditions, the financial covenants and their cure rights, the events of default and the material adverse change clause.

Question 6. Name four term-sheet red flags and the counter for each.

Answer. A floating uncapped rate on a tight coverage ratio: ask for a fixed rate or cap during construction. A short balloon soon after completion: ask for a longer term or an extension option. Fees payable even if the bank declines: ask for fees at or credited against closing. Broad material-adverse-change wording: narrow it to objective tests. Others include cross-collateral over your other assets, an unlimited personal guarantee, and conditions precedent outside your control.

Recap

Cross-border borrowing is decided by four things the headline rate hides. Collateral sits where the land is, so a foreign lender lends against your home assets. Withholding tax with a gross-up raises the effective rate to the quoted rate divided by one minus the withholding rate. Currency mismatch can break coverage without the building doing anything wrong, and tends to arrive with weaker rents. Fees and hedging add the rest. Compare all-in cost and where the risk sits.

A term sheet is the cheapest moment to change a loan. Read it three times, for money, control and personal exposure, mark the red flags, and send one prioritised set of counters. Never pay a non-refundable fee until every condition precedent has been checked against what exists today.

Mr Shabazz, the tool to keep from this week is the all-in comparison table: one column per lender, with rate, gross-up, fees, hedging, security, guarantees, currency and governing law, filled in before rate is discussed. Next week brings it all together: building the package, running lender meetings, managing the loan after closing, and what to do when a loan gets into trouble.

Notice how these lessons chain together. The comparison table from Monday decides which lender you are dealing with; the gross-up from Tuesday and the currency stress from Wednesday decide whether its offer survives your coverage test; and the term-sheet reading from Thursday decides what you are actually agreeing to if it does. A borrower who does them in that order rarely signs a term sheet they later regret.

A closing reminder on the tax and legal content of this week. Every withholding rate, treaty provision and enforcement rule used here was an illustration of how such rules are read, not a statement of the current law in any country. Tax rates and treaties change, conditions and exemptions apply, and two advisers in two countries will each see a different half of the problem. The skill this week builds is knowing which questions to ask and how to put the answers into your model, so that the advice you pay for goes straight into a decision.
checklist: Collateral sits where the land is; foreign lenders lend against home assets.
Effective rate equals quoted rate over one minus the withholding rate with a gross-up.
Currency mismatch can breach coverage with full rent collected.
Match loan currency to income where possible.
Term sheets: money, control, personal exposure.
Check every condition precedent before paying a non-refundable fee.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A family member suggests borrowing at home against the family house to fund your project abroad 'because the rate is lower'. What would you say, in two minutes?
selftest.a: Explain that the lower rate may rise once withholding tax and a gross-up, fees and currency hedging are added, so the all-in cost may be higher; that the loan would be secured on the family house, so a failure abroad would be paid for at home; and that income in a different currency from the loan can breach coverage without the building failing. Propose comparing a project-country facility secured on the building, all-in, before deciding, with advice from tax advisers and lawyers in both countries.

apply: Without notes, compute the effective rate of a 6.5 percent loan under a 15 percent withholding with gross-up, and explain aloud what else you would add to compare it all-in.
